title: Elazar ben Durdaya
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: An awesome story is told of him in Avodah Zarah 17a: there was no prostitute with whom he had not sinned. He heard that there was one prostitute whose fee was a purse full of dinars, and when he came to her, in the course of their conversation she told him that no repentance would help him. Her words, which she spoke without intent, entered his heart like venom; he went from her and wept so much that his soul departed. A heavenly voice went out and said: “Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya is destined for the life of the world to come.” Rabbi wept and said: “There is one who acquires his world in one hour” … “and not only that, but they call them ‘Rabbi.’” Hyman argues that this does not prove that he lived in Rabbi’s time, for Rabbi wept over Ketia bar Shalom, who lived in Rabbi Akiva’s time, as in Avodah Zarah 10b.

notes.text: Hyman argues that Rabbi’s weeping does not establish contemporaneity; the Ketia comparison and chronological inference remain his. No automatic contemporary relationship is admitted.

The consulted Avodah Zarah 17a narrative includes the encounter, appeals to mountains and heavenly bodies, repentance, heavenly voice and Rabbi’s weeping. Hyman abridges it. Rabbi’s reaction is not independently treated as proof of contemporaneity; the Ketia comparison and historical dating remain Hyman’s argument.
